items.title: L13: Stepping from HEO to SEO and Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: The step from HEO to SEO is smaller on paper than the step from SEO to Grade 7, and panels treat them differently. HEO and SEO usually share a behaviour level, so what separates an SEO candidate is more scope, more complexity and more independence: leading bigger pieces of work, handling competing priorities with less direction, and being trusted to represent the team. Evidence that you already work that way is persuasive even if your grade says otherwise. Grade 7 is assessed at the next level up, and the shift is qualitative. A Grade 7 is expected to set direction rather than only deliver it, to lead managers as well as staff, and to make judgements where the evidence is incomplete and the consequences reach beyond the team. Panels look for a change in how you describe your work: from I delivered the project to I decided what the priorities should be, convinced others and accepted accountability for the result. Candidates who describe larger and larger tasks at the same level can be marked as ready for more of the same, not as ready for the grade above. Useful preparation includes taking on work that crosses boundaries, such as a cross-department project, deputising for a senior manager, leading a recruitment round or managing a budget. Time at SEO is not a requirement in most adverts, and the Success Profile assessment is about demonstrated behaviours and not tenure, but panels notice if the whole of your evidence comes from a single narrow context. Seek a sponsor at Grade 7 or above who can see your work.

questions.prompt: HEO and SEO candidates are assessed at the same behaviour level. What mainly separates a strong SEO candidate?

options.text: Greater scope, complexity and independence in the work led
Longer continuous service, which panels treat as a proxy for readiness
A professional qualification that HEO posts do not ask for
A larger number of direct reports in every case

questions.hint: Same level means the difference is scale and independence.

questions.prompt: Why can describing ever larger tasks at the same level fail to convince a Grade 7 panel?

options.text: Grade 7 panels give no weight to the size of the work described
Larger tasks score lower because they involve other people's contributions
Referees at senior grades are unable to verify large pieces of work
It can show readiness for more of the same, not the next level of behaviour

questions.hint: Grade 7 is a qualitative shift, not just larger work.

questions.prompt: Which sentence in an example best signals Grade 7 style evidence?

options.text: I delivered the programme on time and under budget as planned
I supported my manager in completing every action on the plan
Managing a recruitment round and a budget across several teams
I followed the guidance carefully and completed all the actions

questions.hint: Grade 7 evidence shows direction, influence and accountability.

questions.prompt: What does a Grade 7 lead that an SEO normally does not?

options.text: A single project board that meets once a month
Managers as well as staff, working through them
Only the staff in their own immediate team, but more of them
Suppliers and contractors but not departmental colleagues

questions.hint: Leading through others is the step up.

questions.prompt: All your evidence comes from one narrow team. What is the most useful step before a Grade 7 application?

options.text: Wait until you have completed a set number of years at SEO
Move to a lower grade in another team to widen your range
Apply regardless, since breadth is never assessed at Grade 7
Take on cross-boundary work, such as a cross-department project

questions.prompt: What do Grade 7 adverts normally require about time already served at SEO?

options.text: Usually none, since assessment is of demonstrated behaviours rather than tenure
A minimum that the Civil Service Commission sets for all Grade 7 posts
At least three years at SEO, which panels treat as a baseline
A minimum that applies only where the candidate comes from another department

questions.hint: Success Profiles assess evidence, not time served.

questions.prompt: Which piece of work most plausibly gives an SEO Grade 7-level evidence?

options.text: Completing a long run of routine tasks without a single error
Writing guidance that other teams then applied without your input
Leading a recruitment round and managing a budget across several teams
Attending senior meetings as an observer to learn how they work

questions.hint: Cross-team leadership and budget accountability are Grade 7 signals.

questions.prompt: How can a sponsor at Grade 7 or above help an SEO?

options.text: By adding a private note to your sift score for the panel
By seeing your work and opening stretch opportunities
By deciding your result at interview if you are a close call
By moving you into a Grade 7 post without a competition

questions.hint: Sponsors help visibility and opportunity, not outcomes.

questions.prompt: An SEO describes handling competing priorities with little direction and representing the team to senior stakeholders. How would a panel read this?

options.text: As evidence best omitted because stakeholders are confidential
As irrelevant, since independence is not assessed above HEO
As strong evidence of independence and scope, a bridge to Grade 7
As weak evidence, since representing the team is a HEO activity

questions.hint: These are hallmarks of independence and scope.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the HEO to SEO step is accurate?

options.text: It is a step in behaviour level, with Leadership first assessed at SEO
It is a step in scope and independence, because the behaviour level stays the same
It needs a technical qualification in every profession
It needs a move to a different department first

questions.hint: HEO and SEO usually share a behaviour level.

items.title: L13: Reading team structure and stakeholders in a role profile
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A role profile contains clues about the real shape of a job that are easy to miss. The reporting line shows who you answer to and how senior they are: reporting to a Grade 6 or Deputy Director tells you the post sits close to decisions, while reporting to an SEO suggests the post is closer to delivery. The number of direct reports and whether they include managers suggests the leadership scale. Look for the stakeholders: ministers and their private offices, other departments, arm's-length bodies, regulators, local authorities, suppliers or the public. Posts that have regular contact with ministers or senior officials usually expect confident, clear written advice and a calm manner under pressure. Phrases such as lead on, own, be accountable for and shape signal responsibility, while support, assist and contribute signal a more junior role. Look at whether the post is permanent or fixed term, whether there is a line management element, and whether the advert says the post is part of a larger programme with a defined end date. Think about what is not stated. If the profile gives little detail about budget or number of staff, ask the recruiting team. If the grade seems higher than the duties, find out whether the post carries unusual risk, such as national security, a high-profile programme or demanding public contact. Use the clues to choose examples of similar scale: describe working with senior stakeholders if the post demands it, and managing a team if that is the expectation.

questions.prompt: A post reports to a Deputy Director. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The post sits close to senior decisions and carries real responsibility
The post is exempt from open competition
The post is junior and has little real autonomy
The post is temporary and has no leadership element

questions.hint: Senior reporting lines suggest proximity to decisions.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in a profile most strongly signals responsibility at a senior level?

options.text: Contribute to the work of
Provide support to the team on
Assist colleagues with
Be accountable for the delivery of

questions.prompt: What does regular contact with ministers' private offices usually demand?

options.text: A ministerial appointment to the post
Public statements on the department's behalf
Accurate, clear written advice and calm under pressure
Active membership of a political party

questions.hint: Ministerial contact means high standards of advice.

questions.prompt: A profile gives little detail on budget or team size. What is the sensible next step?

options.text: Apply and raise the question only if you reach interview
Ask the recruiting team for more information before applying
Avoid mentioning scale in your application, to stay safe
Assume a medium-sized team and budget and write accordingly

questions.hint: Ask early for facts that affect your evidence.

questions.prompt: A SEO post carries unusual risk, such as a high-profile programme. Why might the grade seem high for the listed duties?

options.text: The grade follows the previous post-holder's pay
The grade was set in error and will be corrected after advert
The advert is intended for external candidates only
Grade can reflect risk and visibility as well as the tasks

questions.hint: Grade reflects job weight, including risk.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter whether the post is part of a programme with a defined end date?

options.text: It affects job security and your options after the programme ends
It means you cannot apply for permanent roles later
It means the post cannot be advertised openly
It means you must already belong to the programme to apply

questions.prompt: Which stakeholder set suggests an outward-facing post?

options.text: Only the department's own finance team
Only the line manager and their deputy
Only colleagues sharing the same office floor
Regulators, local authorities, suppliers and the public

questions.prompt: How should stakeholder clues shape the examples you choose?

options.text: Choose examples from outside work to show breadth
Choose examples with stakeholders of similar seniority and type
Choose examples that avoid stakeholders, to protect confidentiality
Choose the most recent examples whatever their scale

questions.hint: Match scale and type of stakeholders.

questions.prompt: An advert says you will contribute to a programme. How should you read that phrase?

options.text: As a more junior or supporting role than lead or own
As proof that the post has no line management
As a signal that the post is highly senior
As a requirement to hold prior programme experience

questions.hint: Contribute signals support rather than leadership.

questions.prompt: Which clue best suggests a leadership scale beyond one team?

options.text: A shared open-plan working area
A request for flexible working hours
Direct reports who are themselves managers
A requirement for good IT skills

items.title: L13: Leading with the right criteria when many are listed
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Many adverts list several behaviours, strengths and experience requirements, but the sift scores only some. The advert should say which are assessed at each stage, and your strategy should follow. When it names two or three lead criteria for the sift, spend most of your effort there: every word counted against a word limit is better used on a scored criterion than on one that will only be tested at interview. For the remaining criteria, prepare ahead of the interview. If the advert does not say which criteria are scored at sift, assume that any could be, and divide your statement across them, giving the most space to the behaviours listed first or emphasised in the role profile. Within a criterion, choose the example that best matches the level and context of the post: a high-impact example that shows judgement beats three small examples. Avoid padding with generic claims such as I am a strong communicator, because assertions earn little without evidence. Be careful with overlap. If one example is strong on two criteria, use it for the one where it is strongest and pick a separate example for the other, because a panel member scoring both criteria will notice repetition and may suspect thin evidence. Check your own statement against the criteria by highlighting where each is covered. A final check on the word count and the sift instructions can avoid losing marks on technical grounds. Where you are required to give a CV as well, make sure it is consistent with your statement.

questions.prompt: The advert names two lead criteria for the sift. How should you use your word limit?

options.text: Put most of the words behind those two scored criteria
Spend most of the words on your career background
Cover the lead criteria briefly and leave detail for interview
Divide the words equally across every criterion in the advert

questions.hint: Words are best spent on what is scored.

questions.prompt: The advert does not say which criteria are scored at sift. What is the safest assumption?

options.text: None are scored and only the CV is read
Any could be scored, so cover all and favour those emphasised
Only criteria marked desirable are scored
Only the first criterion listed is scored

questions.prompt: Which choice of evidence is usually stronger?

options.text: A list of duties from your last two jobs
A short summary of what the team achieved
Three small examples of routine tasks done well
One high-impact example showing judgement at the right level

questions.prompt: Why is I am a strong communicator a weak use of space?

options.text: It breaches the Code's rule on self-promotion
It is valid only if a manager has confirmed it
It is an assertion with no evidence to score
Most panels mark any self-description as negative

questions.prompt: One example is strong on two criteria. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use it where strongest and choose another for the other criterion
Drop it and use weaker examples to avoid repetition
Use it for both, so the panel sees your best work twice
Keep it for the interview only and leave it out of writing

questions.hint: Variety avoids the appearance of thin evidence.

questions.prompt: A scorer sees the same example used twice. What might they conclude?

options.text: That you have misunderstood the question
That the first example was not true
That evidence for one criterion may be thin
That you have breached copyright in the earlier statement

questions.prompt: What is a useful check on a finished statement?

options.text: Ask a friend to rewrite the weakest answer for you
Read it once for spelling and then submit
Check that the word count exactly matches the limit
Highlight where each criterion is covered and confirm none is missing

questions.prompt: Why check the sift instructions and word limit before submitting?

options.text: Panels ignore any text within the word limit
Technical breaches can lose marks even when the content is strong
The limits apply to external candidates but not internal ones
The instructions are optional guidance only

questions.prompt: A CV and a personal statement are both required. What matters about them?

options.text: The CV should include different facts to add interest
The statement should replace the CV in the scoring
The CV should repeat the statement word for word
They should be consistent and not contradict each other

questions.prompt: Which criteria deserve preparation even though they are not scored at sift?

options.text: Only those scored at sift
Those likely to be tested at interview
None, since the sift decides the final outcome
Only the technical criteria

items.title: L13: Presentations and case studies at senior interviews
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: At HEO, SEO and Grade 7, some interviews include a presentation or a case study alongside the questions. A presentation usually asks you to prepare a short talk, often with slides, on a topic given in advance, followed by questions. It tests Communicating and Influencing, the ability to structure a message, and your knowledge of the subject. Open with your main message, support it with a few well-chosen points, and finish with a recommendation or next step. Keep to the time limit, because overrunning can be marked down. Aim slides at the audience and avoid dense text. Prepare for questions by anticipating weaknesses in your argument. A case study gives you a scenario and asks for analysis or a recommendation, sometimes in writing under timed conditions and sometimes in discussion. It tests judgement, problem solving and written or spoken clarity. Start by identifying the decision to be made, the options and the evidence; weigh costs, risks and benefits; then give a clear recommendation, say what you would do first, and acknowledge uncertainty and trade-offs. Do not describe all the facts back to the panel; they have read them. For both formats, check the technical set-up in advance, ask about reasonable adjustments if needed, and practise aloud in front of someone who will challenge you. Panels respond well to a clear line of argument, honesty about what you do not know and willingness to respond to challenge without defensiveness.

questions.prompt: Which structure suits a short interview presentation?

options.text: Main message first, a few supporting points, then a recommendation
A list of every fact you found followed by questions
A full history of the topic followed by a brief conclusion
A long story about your career leading to a summary

questions.prompt: Why does overrunning the time limit matter?

options.text: It is scored as extra evidence of enthusiasm
It is penalised only when the panel is short of time
It can be marked down and shows poor control of the message
It does not affect the assessment

questions.prompt: What should slides for a panel presentation avoid?

options.text: Short headings with one key chart
A single supporting image where useful
Dense blocks of text that the audience must read
A clear title and final recommendation

questions.prompt: What does a case study mainly test?

options.text: Length of service in the department
Judgement, problem solving and clarity of communication
Knowledge of the work of the previous post-holder
Memory for facts about the department

questions.prompt: What is a good first step in a case study with a decision to make?

options.text: Identify the decision, the options and the evidence
Write the conclusion before reading the evidence
Retell all the facts to the panel in order
Ask the panel which option they prefer

questions.prompt: Why not retell all the facts of the case to the panel?

options.text: The panel will test you on different facts
The facts are confidential and may not be repeated
Repeating facts breaches the interview rules
They have read them and want your analysis and recommendation

questions.prompt: How should you respond when the panel challenges your recommendation?

options.text: By defending the original position at all costs
Calmly, acknowledging uncertainty and explaining your reasoning
By changing your recommendation at once to match theirs
By asking the panel to move to another question

questions.prompt: You need a reasonable adjustment for a presentation. What should you do?

options.text: Ask well in advance using the contact in the advert
Wait until the day and raise it with the panel
Assume it will not be available and say nothing
Raise it only if you do not pass the sift

questions.prompt: Which preparation step is most useful for a presentation?

options.text: Memorising every word of a script
Reading the slides silently to check them
Practising aloud with someone who will challenge you
Practising only on the morning of the interview

questions.hint: Aloud practice with challenge builds readiness.

questions.prompt: What should a good case study recommendation contain?

options.text: A full list of risks with no recommendation
A statement that more information is needed before deciding
A recommendation that avoids all risk
A clear recommendation, a first step and the trade-offs and uncertainties

items.title: L13: Professions, functions and their competency frameworks
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Government Functions guidance
items.body: The Civil Service is organised in professions and cross-government functions as well as departments. A profession, such as digital and data, finance, legal, commercial, project delivery, policy, communications, analysis or operational delivery, brings together people who do similar work across departments and sets standards for skills and careers. Many publish a competency or skills framework that describes what is expected at each grade, along with learning routes and sometimes qualifications. For a person aiming to progress, these frameworks are practical: they tell you what evidence to build at HEO, SEO and Grade 7, and they help you speak the language of a panel when applying for a post in that profession. Some professions use specific job titles and pay arrangements, and some run their own recruitment or talent schemes. Adverts for professional posts may specify technical requirements, such as a qualification or accreditation, which carry weight at sift. A move between professions is possible but may need new evidence: a policy adviser moving into project delivery could use transferable evidence of planning and stakeholder management but would need to show the technical skills the new profession expects, perhaps by taking a certification or a loan. Joining a profession network gives access to events, mentors and vacancy information. Do not assume that a profession's title in one department equals the same grade in another; check the role profile for scope. Professional frameworks do not replace the Success Profiles: both are used.

questions.prompt: What is a profession in the Civil Service sense?

options.text: A team inside one department that carries out a single piece of work for it
A job title that exists in only one department and carries a fixed grade
A group doing similar work across departments with shared standards
A band of staff on the same pay point who share a union

questions.prompt: How can a competency framework help an aspiring HEO?

options.text: It shows what is expected at each grade and so what evidence to build
It replaces the Success Profiles in every professional post and competition
It sets the salary scale that every department must pay the profession
It guarantees promotion once you have completed each stage it lists

questions.prompt: An advert for a professional post lists a qualification as a technical requirement. What does this mean at sift?

options.text: It is waived automatically for existing civil servants applying from within
It carries weight and may be scored or used as a condition
It is tested only at the interview, with no part in the sift
It is a courtesy that panels rarely check, so it need not be evidenced

questions.prompt: A policy adviser wants to move into project delivery. What is the best approach?

options.text: Leave out the policy evidence so the application looks like a fresh start
Wait for the new profession to approach you with a suitable post
Apply on length of service in policy alone and let the panel judge fit
Use transferable evidence and build the profession's technical skills

questions.hint: Show transferable evidence plus new skills.

questions.prompt: Why join a profession network?

options.text: It removes the need to compete for posts that the network advertises
It is compulsory before you can apply for any professional post
It gives access to events, mentors and vacancy information
It gives priority in recruitment to anyone who joins before applying

questions.hint: Networks help with opportunity and information.

questions.prompt: Is a profession's job title in one department the same grade in another?

options.text: Not necessarily, so check the role profile for scope
Always, since a title maps directly to a single grade across government
Only in professions that publish a competency framework for each grade
Only for posts in London, where grading is standardised

questions.prompt: How do professional frameworks relate to Success Profiles?

options.text: Success Profiles apply only to generalist posts, never to specialist ones
Frameworks replace the Success Profiles in professional posts and competitions
Frameworks are used only to set pay and have no part in selection
They complement each other and both can be used

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Civil Service profession or function?

options.text: Public relations, which sits as a separate board outside the professions
Commercial
A customer lounge, which is how a department hosts external visitors
A marketing board, which is a body that each department creates

questions.hint: Commercial is one of the functions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about professional recruitment is accurate?

options.text: Some professions run their own recruitment or talent schemes
Professions have no part in recruitment, which departments alone control
All professions use identical panels and criteria for every vacancy
Professions recruit only from outside government and never internally

questions.hint: Some professions run their own schemes.

questions.prompt: What is a sound reason to move between professions?

options.text: To skip the sift in the new profession because you already know the work
To broaden your experience, if you will build the technical skills needed
To gain a higher salary, since professions always pay more than generalist posts
To avoid assessment against the Success Profiles by using a framework

items.title: L13: Negotiating a promotion offer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental HR policy
items.body: Once a conditional offer arrives, there may still be points to discuss, but they are narrower than in many private-sector jobs. Pay on promotion is usually governed by departmental policy and the pay range for the grade, and the offer letter will state the starting salary. Some departments have rules that place a promoted civil servant at the minimum of the new range or at a set increase, whichever is greater, while others have more discretion. External appointees may also be bound by the range. You can ask how the salary was calculated and whether any allowances, such as a location allowance or a market-related supplement for a shortage skill, apply. Other terms are more flexible. Start date is often negotiable within reason, because it depends on your current employer's notice and the new team's needs. Working pattern, such as part-time or flexible hours, is a legitimate request, and under flexible working rules employees can ask for it from day one, with the employer considering it reasonably. Location and hybrid arrangements are usually set by the post's policy but may allow some flexibility. Ask about probation, the reporting line and induction. Do not make demands that are inconsistent with the Recruitment Principles, such as asking for a different grade or a role not advertised. Keep the tone constructive and get any agreed changes in writing before you resign, because a verbal assurance can be hard to enforce.

questions.prompt: What usually governs pay on promotion in the Civil Service?

options.text: A fixed national percentage increase applied to every promotion
A personal negotiation with the panel chair after the interview has ended
Departmental policy and the pay range for the grade
The salary of the runner-up candidate, which sets the benchmark

questions.prompt: Which question about pay is reasonable?

options.text: Whether you can see the pay of other members of the team to compare
Whether your salary can be matched to the figure another candidate has requested
Whether your pay can be fixed above the maximum of the range
How the starting salary was calculated and whether any allowances apply

questions.prompt: Which term is often negotiable within reason?

options.text: The job title as advertised, which the manager can change before you start
The start date, given notice periods and team needs
The criteria used at selection, which can be reviewed after the offer
The grade of the post, which can be raised if you ask politely

questions.prompt: What can an employee do under flexible working rules?

options.text: Request a flexible arrangement, which the employer must consider reasonably
Insist on whatever pattern of hours you prefer, as the right is absolute
Withdraw from probation to work flexibly from your first day
Ask for a higher grade for the same post, to match your preferred hours

questions.hint: A right to request, not to insist.

questions.prompt: Which request would be inconsistent with the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Asking about the reporting line and who supervises you daily
Asking about the induction arrangements for the first weeks in post
Asking to be appointed to a grade or role that was not advertised
Asking about the probation period and how it is assessed

questions.hint: Appointments must follow competition for advertised posts.

questions.prompt: When should an agreed change to terms be put in writing?

options.text: Never, as verbal agreements between professionals are binding
Only if there is a later dispute about what was agreed
After you have started in the new post, once you have settled in
Before you resign from your current post

questions.prompt: Why might a market-related supplement be offered?

options.text: To compensate for a lower grade than your previous post
To cover the cost of travel to interviews and assessments
To reward length of service, which is paid to long-serving staff
To attract people with a shortage skill

questions.prompt: Which question about probation is sensible?

options.text: How long it lasts and how performance will be reviewed
Whether probation applies to the members of the interview panel
Whether the probation result can be agreed in advance in writing
Whether you can be excused from probation because of your experience

questions.prompt: How should you approach negotiation overall?

options.text: By waiting until you have started the job before raising anything
Constructively, with narrow, reasonable asks confirmed in writing
By threatening to withdraw unless every one of your requests is met
By comparing your pay with colleagues' pay in the new team

questions.prompt: Why can a verbal assurance be risky?

options.text: Verbal assurances override the terms in the written offer letter
Verbal assurances bind the whole department, whoever made them
It can be hard to enforce if the manager changes or memories differ
Verbal assurances are unlawful in recruitment and therefore void

items.title: L13: Managing your application alongside your current job
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: Applying for a new post while employed raises practical and ethical questions. Applications usually ask for a referee, often your current line manager, but references are normally taken up only after an offer. You may be asked at interview about your current performance, so keep your manager informed if you want their support and trust them with confidential information. Whether to tell your manager before applying is a judgement: telling them can build goodwill and lead to support, while some people prefer to wait until they reach interview or receive an offer. Do not lie about the reason for time off. Use annual leave, flexi-time or authorised time off for interviews, according to your department's rules, and be honest if asked. Do your application in your own time, not on duty, and use your own device or personal account where policy requires, because using work time or systems for personal career purposes can breach local rules. Do not use confidential information or colleagues' work as evidence without permission: describe the contribution and results in terms that do not reveal sensitive details. Maintain your standard of work while the application is in progress, because you will probably need your manager's reference and your current reputation matters. If your manager obstructs a legitimate move, such as by refusing to release you without reason, raise it with HR or the nominated officer and, if necessary, use the department's grievance procedure. Be polite and professional with everyone throughout.

questions.prompt: When are references normally taken up?

options.text: Before the interview, so that the panel can check your claims
Only if the panel is divided between two close candidates
After a conditional offer has been made
At the sift stage, so that the panel can weigh your current performance

questions.prompt: What is the sensible view on telling your manager before you apply?

options.text: HR will always tell your manager automatically when you apply
You must never tell your manager until after you have left the post
You must always tell your manager before you apply, as a matter of courtesy and rules
It is a judgement call: telling them can build support, but some wait

questions.prompt: How should you take time off for an interview?

options.text: Say it is for a medical appointment
Annual leave, flexi or authorised time, with honesty if asked
Report sick and attend the interview
Take unpaid leave without asking

questions.prompt: Where should you prepare your application?

options.text: In your own time, on your own device where policy requires
Using your manager's account so that the application is tracked
On duty using the office systems, since it is convenient and quick
During meetings that you consider unnecessary to your own work

questions.hint: Do not use work time for personal career purposes.

questions.prompt: Can you use a colleague's work as evidence without permission?

options.text: You can use it if you lead the team, as you are responsible for its output
You can use anything done in your team, because it all belongs to the department
You should not use confidential details or colleagues' work without permission
You can use it if the work is old enough to be no longer sensitive

questions.prompt: Why keep your standard of work high during an application?

options.text: Your sift score will be set by your most recent appraisal rating
The panel will observe your daily work during the competition
Your leave will be refused if your standards drop at all
You may need your manager's reference and your reputation matters

questions.prompt: Your manager refuses to release you for a legitimate move without good reason. What should you do?

options.text: Raise it with HR or the nominated officer and use the grievance procedure if needed
Quietly reduce your effort at work until the manager relents
Resign first and then apply, so that you are free to move
Ask the interview panel to contact your manager and settle the matter

questions.prompt: Which statement about describing a team achievement is most appropriate?

options.text: Include the confidential figures so that your evidence is convincing
Describe your contribution and results without revealing sensitive details
Hide that it was a team effort so that the credit appears to be yours
Describe the whole team's work in full, naming each colleague involved

questions.prompt: How should you behave with colleagues while applying?

options.text: Competitively, so that colleagues see how much you want the job
By lobbying colleagues to speak well of you to the panel
By sharing your interview questions with colleagues who may also apply
Politely and professionally, avoiding gossip about the competition

questions.prompt: Is it acceptable to give a false reason for needing time off for an interview?

options.text: It is acceptable if it avoids awkward questions from your manager
It is acceptable if the interview is important enough to your career
It is not, since honesty is expected under the Civil Service Code
It is acceptable if your manager has been unhelpful about the move

items.title: L13: Timing a move and planning the return from a temporary post
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental HR policy
items.body: People on a loan, secondment or temporary promotion face timing decisions that can shape their career. Plan the return before you go, and revisit the plan halfway through, because vacancies, reporting lines and your own goals can change. A common mistake is to wait until the final weeks to think about what comes next. Start talking to your home department three to six months before the end, share what you have learned and ask what posts will be available. If you want to apply for a permanent post at the host, check the rules: the host must run a fair competition, and you may be eligible only if the advert is open to your department. If your period is extended, ask how and why: an extension should have a clear purpose and a new end date. Consider the effect of repeated extensions on fairness to others and on your own prospects, because long temporary spells can be questioned. Think about the evidence you are building and keep it up to date. A temporary promotion gives you recent evidence at the higher grade, which is most persuasive in the months afterwards, so time an application for a permanent post when the evidence is fresh. If you are to return to a lower grade, it can be demotivating, so plan for it by seeking stretch work, and by agreeing objectives with your manager. If you are considering resigning to take the temporary post permanently elsewhere, check the terms, pension and continuous service implications first.

questions.prompt: When should you start planning your return from a loan?

options.text: Only if you become unhappy at the host and want to leave
Before you go, revisiting the plan midway
After you have returned, once the home department knows your needs
In the final week, when the end date is certain and the host is winding down

questions.prompt: How far ahead of the end should you speak to your home department?

options.text: Around three to six months before
On your last day, when your results are clearest to the host
Only when your home department contacts you first
A year after the period ends, when the home department has settled

questions.prompt: You want a permanent post at the host. What should you check?

options.text: That the host will run a fair competition and that you are eligible to apply
That the host can appoint you without a competition if the manager wants to
That the host team likes you enough to ask you to stay
That your home manager will approve the move automatically

questions.prompt: Why should an extension have a clear purpose and new end date?

options.text: To avoid paying you extra for the longer period
To avoid open-ended temporary arrangements that raise fairness concerns
To meet a tax requirement on temporary arrangements
To ensure you cannot apply for the post once it is advertised

questions.prompt: What is a risk of repeated extensions?

options.text: They stop you from applying for other roles
They create a right to the permanent post
They can be questioned for fairness and may limit your prospects
They increase your salary automatically

questions.prompt: When is evidence from a temporary promotion most persuasive?

options.text: Five years later, when the panel has had time to forget the context
Only in the first week of acting up, when the evidence is new
Never, since evidence from a temporary post cannot be counted
In the months afterwards, while it is fresh

questions.prompt: Which is a useful way to handle a return to a lower grade?

options.text: Ask for the higher grade to be kept in your substantive post
Refuse to return until you have been promoted into a higher post
Seek stretch work and agree objectives with your manager
Resign from the Civil Service, as returning is a step backwards

questions.prompt: Before resigning to take a temporary post elsewhere permanently, what should you check?

options.text: The performance record of the previous post-holder in the new job
The facilities for staff parking and canteen at the new site
The size of the new building and the rooms available to the team
Terms, pension and continuous service implications

questions.prompt: What is a common mistake about the end of a temporary post?

options.text: Staying in touch with your home department, which can distract the host
Waiting until the final weeks to think about what comes next
Planning too early, so that you have little to show at the end
Writing down what you have learned, which risks revealing confidences

questions.prompt: What should you share with your home department before the end?

options.text: What you have learned and the evidence you have built
Confidential information from the host that might help the home department
A request that you be promoted automatically when you return
Complaints about the host staff, to explain why you want to leave

items.title: L13: Candidate conflicts when someone you know is on the panel
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Because the Civil Service is large but interconnected, you may find that someone you know sits on your panel. This is not unusual, and it does not mean the process is unfair, but how it is handled matters. As a candidate, you should declare the relationship if the advert or application form asks for it, and you may do so in any case if it is close, such as a family member, close friend or a former line manager. Do not try to arrange a particular panel member or to influence them. The panel chair, once informed, will consider whether the relationship is a conflict of interest that requires the person to step down or whether safeguards, such as independent scoring by the others, are enough. Typical safeguards include the person not scoring that candidate, a panel with a majority of independent members, and a clear record of the decision. A previous working relationship does not automatically exclude someone, because a person who has worked with you may be the best judge of some evidence, but a close personal or financial tie usually does. If you discover a conflict after the competition has started, raise it promptly with the HR contact or the chair. Do not use the relationship as an advantage, for example by asking for hints, and do not assume the panel member will favour you. If you are unsure whether to declare, declare: it is better to be open than to have the outcome challenged later.

questions.prompt: You know a panel member from a previous team. What is your first duty as a candidate?

options.text: Withdraw from the competition so that no issue can arise
Declare the relationship if asked, and consider declaring it anyway if it is close
Say nothing, because mentioning it might harm your chances
Ask the panel member to give you a favourable score because you know each other

questions.prompt: Who decides whether a relationship requires a panel member to step down?

options.text: The candidate, who knows the relationship best
The Civil Service Commission, in every case before the interview
The panel member's line manager, who knows the circumstances
The panel chair, with HR advice

questions.prompt: Which is a typical safeguard?

options.text: The person with the connection does not score that candidate
The candidate chooses which panel member should assess them
The panel member scores last so that others cannot be influenced
The relationship is kept from other panel members to avoid embarrassment

questions.prompt: Does a previous working relationship automatically exclude someone from the panel?

options.text: It does only if the panel member is at a higher grade than the candidate
It does only if the candidate asks for the person to be removed
It does not, but a close personal or financial tie usually does
It always does, however slight the previous contact was

questions.prompt: What should you do if you discover a conflict after the process has started?

options.text: Tell the other candidates so that they can decide whether to object
Raise it promptly with the HR contact or the chair
Contact the panel member privately to agree how to handle it
Wait until the result, in case the issue turns out not to matter

questions.prompt: Which candidate action is improper?

options.text: Following the chair's instruction about the panel arrangement
Keeping a record of the declaration you made
Asking a panel member for hints about the questions
Declaring a family connection when you first realise it exists

questions.prompt: Why is it better to declare when unsure?

options.text: It means that you cannot be scored by that panel at all
It allows you to choose a panel that you consider suitable
It guarantees that the panel will give you extra marks for honesty
It prevents the outcome being challenged later for non-disclosure

questions.prompt: What should you assume about a panel member you know personally?

options.text: Nothing: do not assume favour and do not rely on it
That the relationship matters less because you are an internal candidate
That they can influence the other members if they are senior enough
That they will favour you because they know your work and ability

questions.prompt: A panel includes a majority of independent members and a record is kept. What does this support?

options.text: Confidence that the decision was fair despite the relationship
A reason for the candidate to ignore the declaration already made
The removal of any need for the panel to keep notes
A guarantee that the candidate will be successful at the interview

questions.prompt: Which relationship is most likely to require a panel member to step down?

options.text: A person who works on a different floor of the same building
A close family member or financial tie to the candidate
A previous colleague who worked in a different team some years ago
Someone who attended the same training course as the candidate

items.title: L13: Talent schemes, development programmes and fair selection
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; departmental talent guidance
items.body: Talent schemes and development programmes, such as accelerated development or leadership schemes, aim to prepare people for higher grades. Many are run by departments, professions or across government, and some are open to staff at specific grades with a nomination or an application process. Because they can give access to experience, networks and often faster promotion, selection to them should itself be fair. Good practice includes publishing the criteria, advertising places widely, using a consistent assessment, and recording the decision. Some schemes ask for manager nomination, which can create a bottleneck if managers do not nominate people who are less visible; departments should therefore allow self-nomination or balance it with other routes. It is important to know what a scheme offers and does not offer. Selection to a development scheme does not by itself give promotion; promotion to a higher grade still needs fair and open competition on merit, though participants may be better prepared or may have access to more stretch opportunities. Some schemes use positive action in a lawful way, for example by encouraging applications from groups that are under-represented, but selection must still be on merit. If you are considering a scheme, read the eligibility, the time commitment, whether your manager's support is required, and what the scheme says about outcomes. Ask previous participants for their view. If you believe the selection to a scheme is unfair, use the department's complaints route.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a talent or development scheme?

options.text: To give extra pay to the staff who are selected
To replace the normal recruitment competitions for higher grades
To prepare participants for higher grades through experience and development
To guarantee that selected staff will be promoted at the end

questions.prompt: Which practice makes selection to a scheme fair?

options.text: Places offered to whoever is nominated first
Places given to the longest-serving applicants
Places allocated privately by managers who know the candidates
Published criteria, wide advertising, consistent assessment and records

questions.prompt: Why can manager nomination create a bottleneck?

options.text: Managers always nominate every member of staff in the team
Managers have no say in nominations, so no bottleneck can arise
Managers are not allowed to nominate under the Recruitment Principles
Managers may not nominate people who are less visible

questions.hint: Nomination can exclude less visible staff.

questions.prompt: Does selection to a development scheme give promotion?

options.text: It does not by itself, since promotion needs a fair and open competition
It gives promotion automatically at the end of the scheme
It gives promotion only to the participants who finish first
It gives promotion if your manager agrees it is deserved

questions.prompt: Which approach to positive action is lawful?

options.text: Lowering the criteria for those groups to increase numbers
Encouraging applications from under-represented groups while still selecting on merit
Excluding people who are not in the group being encouraged
Selecting people because of a protected characteristic, regardless of merit

questions.prompt: What should you read before applying to a scheme?

options.text: The pay scale for the department and the pay of past participants
The profile of previous participants and their later grades
Eligibility, time commitment, manager support and outcomes
The CVs of the panel members who will select you

questions.prompt: Who can give useful insight about a scheme?

options.text: Newspaper reports about the scheme and its popularity
Previous participants
The panel, since only they know how the scheme works
Colleagues who have never applied and so can be objective

questions.prompt: What should you do if you think the selection was unfair?

options.text: Use the department's complaints route
Post your concerns publicly so that the department responds
Resign from the scheme and from your post
Contact the panel directly and ask them to reconsider the decision

questions.prompt: How can departments reduce nomination bottlenecks?

options.text: Abolish the scheme and rely on normal competitions only
Choose participants by lot so that no one decides
Ask managers to nominate more of the people they already know
Allow self-nomination or balance nomination with other routes

questions.prompt: Which of these is a benefit of schemes besides promotion?

options.text: Automatic posts at the next grade up
Higher pay without any change of grade
Networks and stretch opportunities
A guaranteed exemption from probation in your next post

items.title: L13: Exceptions, reporting and the Commission's oversight
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Commission annual reports
items.body: The Recruitment Principles do not only apply to individual vacancies; they also set out how the Commission oversees departments. Departments must keep records of their recruitment and must be able to show that they have followed the Principles. When a department uses an exception, such as a short-term appointment or a secondment, it must record the reason and, in some cases, report it. The Commission audits departments by sampling recruitment, reviewing records and speaking to people involved. It publishes the results and may identify weaknesses, for example where a department has relied too much on exceptions or where records are poor. It also publishes annual reports that describe trends and concerns, and it holds departments to account through engagement with permanent secretaries and, where needed, through reports to Parliament. A department that wants to use an exception not covered by the Principles needs the Commission's approval. Where a department has breached the Principles, the Commission can ask it to explain, make recommendations and follow up on whether they are acted on. The Commission does not run recruitment itself and does not appoint staff. For candidates, this oversight is why records matter and why it is worth asking departments to explain decisions: a department that can show a clear process is more likely to be fair. If you work in HR or on a panel, keep accurate records, because the Commission may ask for them.

questions.prompt: What must departments be able to show about their recruitment?

options.text: That all its posts were permanent and advertised externally
That every appointment it made was internal and of existing staff
That they followed the Recruitment Principles, supported by records
That candidates were chosen by seniority within each team

questions.prompt: How does the Commission check compliance?

options.text: By appointing the successful candidate
By sampling recruitment, reviewing records and speaking to staff
By running recruitment itself
By interviewing every candidate

questions.prompt: What happens when a department uses an exception?

options.text: It must record the reason and in some cases report it
It must hold an open competition anyway, so the exception is redundant
It must stop recruiting until the Commission has given approval
It must ask the candidate to agree to the exception in writing

questions.prompt: Which action needs the Commission's approval?

options.text: Appointing a candidate who meets the criteria on merit
Giving feedback to an unsuccessful candidate
Advertising a vacancy on Civil Service Jobs
Using an exception not covered by the Principles

questions.prompt: Which of these does the Commission not do?

options.text: Run recruitment itself or appoint staff
Report to Parliament about its work and concerns
Publish the results of its audits of departments
Make recommendations to departments after audits

questions.hint: It oversees but does not recruit.

questions.prompt: What does the Commission's annual report describe?

options.text: The pay and grading of all civil servants across departments
Trends and concerns in recruitment across departments
The full list of vacancies advertised in the year
The names of all unsuccessful candidates in competitions

questions.prompt: Why does oversight matter to candidates?

options.text: It ensures that all candidates who apply will pass the sift
It removes the need for departments to give feedback
It guarantees every candidate a job once oversight is applied
Departments that can show a clear process are more likely to be fair

questions.prompt: What can the Commission do after a breach?

options.text: Choose a new candidate for the post itself
Change the panel's scores to a fairer outcome
Ask the department to explain, make recommendations and follow up
Dismiss the HR director of the department concerned

questions.prompt: What is a sign of weak practice that an audit might find?

options.text: Over-reliance on exceptions or poor records
Clear published criteria used across every competition
Consistent scoring approaches with notes kept
Written feedback offered to every candidate on request

questions.prompt: Why should HR staff and panel members keep accurate records?

options.text: They are shared with all candidates after each competition
They are destroyed the day after the decision is made
They are used to calculate pay for the panel members
The Commission may ask for them

items.title: L13: Resilience and learning across several rounds of rejection
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A run of rejections is common, especially at HEO and above, where competition is strong and pass marks are set against the quality of the field. The way you respond shapes how quickly you progress. Treat your applications as a series of experiments, not a series of verdicts. Keep a simple record: the post, the grade, the stage you reached, the scores or feedback and what you changed afterwards. After five or six applications, look at the pattern. If you are failing at sift, the problem is usually in the written evidence, in the choice of examples or in how well they match the criteria. If you are failing at interview, look at structure, depth, evidence of your own role and whether you were confident in the strengths questions. If you are consistently near the mark, small improvements can make a difference; if you are well below, consider whether you are applying at the right grade or need more evidence first. Use the people around you: a mentor, a sponsor or colleagues who have succeeded can read your answers or run a mock interview. Protect your wellbeing, because repeated disappointment can lower confidence: take time away, remind yourself of your achievements and keep other sources of purpose. Do not take feedback personally, but do not dismiss it either. Decide in advance what you will do if the next application is unsuccessful, such as taking a break, seeking a stretch role or applying for a different type of post.

questions.prompt: How should you treat a series of applications?

options.text: As a contest against your colleagues in the same grade
As a series of verdicts on whether you are good enough
As a series of experiments you can learn from
As a lottery that you cannot influence by what you do

questions.prompt: What is useful to record about each application?

options.text: Only whether you were successful
The post, grade, stage reached, feedback and what you changed
Only the name of the panel chair
Only the date of the outcome

questions.prompt: If you fail repeatedly at sift, where is the problem most likely?

options.text: In your choice of referees, as they affect the sift score
In your interview technique, since the sift only checks eligibility
In your security clearance, which is checked at sift
In the written evidence, example choice or match to the criteria

questions.prompt: If you are consistently near the pass mark, what is most useful?

options.text: Small improvements to evidence and delivery
Change profession immediately, since the current one is not working
Apply only to lower grades from now on
Stop applying until the next advert appears at your grade

questions.prompt: If you are well below the pass mark, what should you consider?

options.text: Ignore the feedback, since it reflects one panel's view
Apply to more posts at the same grade, using the same approach
Whether you are applying at the right grade or need more evidence first
Ask the panel to lower the pass mark for your next application

questions.prompt: Who can help you improve between applications?

options.text: A person who dislikes the process
A mentor, sponsor or successful colleague who reviews your answers
Anyone who has not applied
The panel that rejected you

questions.prompt: Which action protects wellbeing?

options.text: Avoiding all feedback until you feel better
Telling colleagues that you are not bothered by the outcome
Applying to more jobs immediately, to keep up momentum
Taking time away and reminding yourself of your achievements

questions.prompt: How should you treat feedback emotionally?

options.text: Ignore it unless it is positive and encouraging
Do not take it personally, but do not dismiss it
Take it as proof that you will not be promoted
Dismiss it as one person's view and move on

questions.prompt: Why decide in advance what you will do after another rejection?

options.text: It removes the need to ask for feedback after each outcome
It guarantees that your next application will be successful
It helps you respond constructively rather than reactively
It stops you from applying for any further posts

questions.prompt: After five or six applications, what should you do?

options.text: Examine the pattern across them
Apply for the same post again, since the panel may change
Stop applying, since six unsuccessful attempts is enough evidence
Change everything at once, so that something is bound to work
